claim: Connexins form hexameric channels in the plasma membrane known as hemichannels.
source: Connexins form hexameric channels in the plasma membrane known as hemichannels, which can either function as regulated passageways between the cell and its environment, or dock with a hemichannel from another cell to form a dodecameric intercellular channel, or gap junction channel (GJC).
evidence: This is a well-established structural description of connexin organization supported by the scientific literature.

claim: Hemichannels can dock with a hemichannel from another cell to form a dodecameric intercellular channel or gap junction channel (GJC).
source: Connexins form hexameric channels in the plasma membrane known as hemichannels, which can either function as regulated passageways between the cell and its environment, or dock with a hemichannel from another cell to form a dodecameric intercellular channel, or gap junction channel (GJC).
evidence: This describes the structural assembly of gap junction channels from hemichannels, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Connexins have been shown to be directly regulated by voltage.
source: Connexins have been shown to be directly regulated by various stimuli such as voltage (Valiunas, 2002; Young and Peracchia, 2004), pH (Bevans and Harris, 1999; Khan et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2007) or indirectly via intracellular calcium ion concentrations (Peracchia, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Connexins have been shown to be directly regulated by pH.
source: Connexins have been shown to be directly regulated by various stimuli such as voltage (Valiunas, 2002; Young and Peracchia, 2004), pH (Bevans and Harris, 1999; Khan et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2007) or indirectly via intracellular calcium ion concentrations (Peracchia, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Connexins can be regulated indirectly via intracellular calcium ion concentrations.
source: Connexins have been shown to be directly regulated by various stimuli such as voltage (Valiunas, 2002; Young and Peracchia, 2004), pH (Bevans and Harris, 1999; Khan et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2007) or indirectly via intracellular calcium ion concentrations (Peracchia, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Recent reports based on structural data suggest that lipids may be involved in connexin regulation.
source: Recent reports based on structural data also suggest that lipids may be involved in regulation (Lee et al., 2023a; Lee et al., 2023b; Qi et al., 2023a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent structural studies.

claim: Connexin26 (Cx26) can be regulated by the direct action of physiological concentrations of carbon dioxide independently of pH.
source: We have shown, however, that connexin26 (Cx26) and other similar β-connexins (Cx30, Cx32) can be regulated by the direct action of physiological concentrations of carbon dioxide independently of pH (Huckstepp et al., 2010; Meigh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: Other similar β-connexins (Cx30, Cx32) can be regulated by the direct action of physiological concentrations of carbon dioxide independently of pH.
source: We have shown, however, that connexin26 (Cx26) and other similar β-connexins (Cx30, Cx32) can be regulated by the direct action of physiological concentrations of carbon dioxide independently of pH (Huckstepp et al., 2010; Meigh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: Mutants of Cx26 are a leading cause of congenital deafness.
source: Mutants of Cx26 are a leading cause of congenital deafness (Xu and Nicholson, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published review.

claim: Many Cx26 mutations are non-syndromic.
source: While many of the mutations are non-syndromic, others lead to severe diseases such as keratitis ichthyosis deafness syndrome (KIDS) (Xu and Nicholson, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published review.

claim: Some Cx26 mutations lead to severe diseases such as keratitis ichthyosis deafness syndrome (KIDS).
source: While many of the mutations are non-syndromic, others lead to severe diseases such as keratitis ichthyosis deafness syndrome (KIDS) (Xu and Nicholson, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published review.

claim: Hemichannels have different properties to GJCs.
source: Hemichannels are known to have different properties to GJCs (Stout et al., 2004) and our previous results show that an increase in the partial pressure of CO2 (PCO2) will open Cx26 hemichannels (Huckstepp et al., 2010) but close Cx26 GJCs (Nijjar et al., 2021), which are open under physiological conditions of PCO2.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: An increase in the partial pressure of CO2 (PCO2) will open Cx26 hemichannels.
source: Hemichannels are known to have different properties to GJCs (Stout et al., 2004) and our previous results show that an increase in the partial pressure of CO2 (PCO2) will open Cx26 hemichannels (Huckstepp et al., 2010) but close Cx26 GJCs (Nijjar et al., 2021), which are open under physiological conditions of PCO2.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: An increase in the partial pressure of CO2 (PCO2) will close Cx26 GJCs.
source: Hemichannels are known to have different properties to GJCs (Stout et al., 2004) and our previous results show that an increase in the partial pressure of CO2 (PCO2) will open Cx26 hemichannels (Huckstepp et al., 2010) but close Cx26 GJCs (Nijjar et al., 2021), which are open under physiological conditions of PCO2.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Cx26 GJCs are open under physiological conditions of PCO2.
source: Hemichannels are known to have different properties to GJCs (Stout et al., 2004) and our previous results show that an increase in the partial pressure of CO2 (PCO2) will open Cx26 hemichannels (Huckstepp et al., 2010) but close Cx26 GJCs (Nijjar et al., 2021), which are open under physiological conditions of PCO2.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: There are 20 connexin genes in the human genome.
source: There are 20 connexin genes in the human genome (Abascal and Zardoya, 2013) and several structures have now been published (Bennett et al., 2016; Brotherton et al., 2022; Flores et al., 2020; Khan et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2023a; Lee et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2023b; Maeda et al., 2009; Myers et al., 2018; Qi et al., 2023a; Qi et al., 2023b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The connexin subunit consists of four transmembrane helices (TMs) with a cytoplasmic N-terminal helix that in the hexameric arrangement of the hemichannel points towards the central pore.
source: The connexin subunit, which is common to all, consists of four transmembrane helices (TMs) with a cytoplasmic N-terminal helix that in the hexameric arrangement of the hemichannel points towards the central pore (Maeda et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published crystal structure.

claim: In structures of the dodecameric GJC, the extracellular part involved in docking is well defined, whereas the cytoplasmic region is much more variable.
source: In structures of the dodecameric GJC, the extracellular part involved in docking is well defined, whereas the cytoplasmic region is much more variable.
evidence: This is an observation based on comparison of multiple published structures.

claim: A large cytoplasmic loop between TM2 and TM3, shown to be involved in regulation, has not been visible in any structure.
source: A large cytoplasmic loop between TM2 and TM3, shown to be involved in regulation, has not been visible in any structure.
evidence: This is an observation based on comparison of published structures and knowledge of the regulatory role of this loop.

claim: The position of the N-terminal helix is thought to be important in the regulation of channel permeability.
source: The position of the N-terminal helix is thought to be important in the regulation of channel permeability.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural observations and knowledge of channel function.

claim: For human Cx26 GJCs, the position of the N-terminus is dependent on PCO2 at constant pH.
source: We have shown previously for human Cx26 GJCs, that the position of the N-terminus is dependent on PCO2 at constant pH (Brotherton et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Under conditions of high PCO2 the conformation of Cx26 was biased towards a conformation where the N-terminus protrudes radially into the pore to form a constriction at the centre (NConst).
source: By examining structures from protein vitrified at different levels of PCO2, we observed that under conditions of high PCO2 the conformation of the protein was biased towards a conformation where the N-terminus protrudes radially into the pore to form a constriction at the centre (NConst).
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' previous structural observations.

claim: Two distinct conformations of Cx26 were seen with the predominant difference between them in the cytoplasmic portion of TM2.
source: Two distinct conformations of the protein were seen with the predominant difference between them in the cytoplasmic portion of TM2 (Brotherton et al., 2022) where an anticlockwise rotation of TM2 correlated with more definition of the density for the N-terminus.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' previous structural observations.

claim: An anticlockwise rotation of TM2 correlated with more definition of the density for the N-terminus.
source: Two distinct conformations of the protein were seen with the predominant difference between them in the cytoplasmic portion of TM2 (Brotherton et al., 2022) where an anticlockwise rotation of TM2 correlated with more definition of the density for the N-terminus.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' previous structural observations.

claim: Under low PCO2 conditions the conformation with the more defined N-terminus was not observed and the channel appeared more open (NFlex).
source: On the other hand, under low PCO2 conditions the conformation with the more defined N-terminus was not observed and the channel appeared more open (NFlex).
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' previous structural observations.

claim: The regulation of hemichannel opening by CO2 is hypothesised to be through a carbamylation reaction of a specific lysine.
source: Based on a wealth of mutational data it has been hypothesised that the regulation of hemichannel opening by CO2 is through a carbamylation reaction of a specific lysine (Meigh et al., 2015; Meigh et al., 2013; Nijjar et al., 2021).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations to mutational studies.

claim: Carbamylation is a reversible and highly labile reaction of CO2.
source: This post-translational modification is a reversible and highly labile reaction of CO2 (Lorimer, 1983) that effectively changes the charge of a neutral lysine residue to make it negative.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study on carbamylation.

claim: Carbamylation effectively changes the charge of a neutral lysine residue to make it negative.
source: This post-translational modification is a reversible and highly labile reaction of CO2 (Lorimer, 1983) that effectively changes the charge of a neutral lysine residue to make it negative.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the chemical nature of carbamylation.

claim: A 'carbamylation motif' was identified in CO2-sensitive connexins.
source: A so-called 'carbamylation motif' was identified in CO2-sensitive connexins (Dospinescu et al., 2019; Meigh et al., 2013) that when introduced into a related CO2-insensitive connexin rendered the protein CO2-sensitive (Meigh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: When the carbamylation motif was introduced into a related CO2-insensitive connexin, it rendered the protein CO2-sensitive.
source: A so-called 'carbamylation motif' was identified in CO2-sensitive connexins (Dospinescu et al., 2019; Meigh et al., 2013) that when introduced into a related CO2-insensitive connexin rendered the protein CO2-sensitive (Meigh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: In Cx26 the carbamylation motif has the sequence K125VRIEG130.
source: In Cx26 this motif has the sequence K125VRIEG130.
evidence: This is a specific sequence identification based on the protein structure and sequence.

claim: In the crystal structure of the Cx26 GJC, Lys125 is positioned near to the N-terminus of TM3 within ~6 Å of Arg104 of TM2 of the neighbouring subunit.
source: In the crystal structure of the Cx26 GJC that was published in 2009 (Maeda et al., 2009), Lys125, which is conserved amongst β-connexins that are known to be modulated by CO2 (Dospinescu et al., 2019), is positioned near to the N-terminus of TM3 within ~6 Å of Arg104 of TM2 of the neighbouring subunit, at either side of the disordered cytoplasmic loop.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of a published crystal structure.

claim: Lys125 is conserved amongst β-connexins that are known to be modulated by CO2.
source: In the crystal structure of the Cx26 GJC that was published in 2009 (Maeda et al., 2009), Lys125, which is conserved amongst β-connexins that are known to be modulated by CO2 (Dospinescu et al., 2019), is positioned near to the N-terminus of TM3 within ~6 Å of Arg104 of TM2 of the neighbouring subunit, at either side of the disordered cytoplasmic loop.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: It was suggested that upon carbamylation, the negative charge of the modified lysine would attract Arg104 causing a conformational change.
source: It was suggested that upon carbamylation, the negative charge of the modified lysine would attract Arg104 causing a conformational change (Meigh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: In hemichannels, mutation of Lys125 to glutamate (K125E) results in constitutively open hemichannels consistent with elevated PCO2.
source: In hemichannels, mutation of Lys125 to glutamate, so mimicking the charge of the carbamylated lysine (K125E), results in constitutively open hemichannels consistent with elevated PCO2, whereas the corresponding K125R mutation results in hemichannels that cannot be opened by CO2 (Meigh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The K125R mutation results in hemichannels that cannot be opened by CO2.
source: In hemichannels, mutation of Lys125 to glutamate, so mimicking the charge of the carbamylated lysine (K125E), results in constitutively open hemichannels consistent with elevated PCO2, whereas the corresponding K125R mutation results in hemichannels that cannot be opened by CO2 (Meigh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: In GJCs, the K125R mutation results in the protein not closing in response to CO2.
source: In GJCs, the K125R mutation results in the protein not closing in response to CO2, though importantly, this mutation does not prevent closure by acidification (Nijjar et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The K125R mutation does not prevent closure of GJCs by acidification.
source: In GJCs, the K125R mutation results in the protein not closing in response to CO2, though importantly, this mutation does not prevent closure by acidification (Nijjar et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Previous structures demonstrated an effect of PCO2 on the conformation of Cx26.
source: While our previous structures (Brotherton et al., 2022) demonstrated an effect of PCO2 on the conformation of the protein, neither Lys125 nor Arg104 were visible in the density.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: In previous structures, neither Lys125 nor Arg104 were visible in the density.
source: While our previous structures (Brotherton et al., 2022) demonstrated an effect of PCO2 on the conformation of the protein, neither Lys125 nor Arg104 were visible in the density.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: By solubilising the protein in LMNG rather than DDM, much improved density for the cytoplasmic region of the protein was obtained.
source: By solubilising the protein in the detergent lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG) rather than dodecyl β-D-maltoside (DDM), we obtain much improved density for the cytoplasmic region of the protein.
evidence: This is a methodological observation from the current study.

claim: Two conformationally diverse structures of Cx26 were refined showing much more defined differences in the cytoplasmic region than observed previously.
source: We refine two conformationally diverse structures of the protein, where we see much more defined differences in the cytoplasmic region of the protein than we were able to observe previously.
evidence: This is a result from the current study.

claim: The data suggest a mechanism for closure involving the concerted movements of TM2 and the KVRIEG motif.
source: These data suggest a mechanism for closure involving the concerted movements of TM2 and the KVRIEG motif.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data from the current study.

claim: The structure with the K125E mutation matches the more closed conformation of the protein.
source: We show that the structure with the K125E mutation matches the more closed conformation of the protein.
evidence: This is a result from the current study.

claim: Refinement with D6 symmetry imposed resulted in a map with a nominal resolution of 2.0 Å for Cx26 vitrified at a PCO2 corresponding to 90 mmHg.
source: Refinement with D6 symmetry imposed resulted in a map with a nominal resolution of 2.0 Å as defined by gold standard Fourier shell correlations (FSC) (Rosenthal and Henderson, 2003; Scheres, 2012; Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is a technical result from the cryo-EM data processing.

claim: The results from classification were broadly in line with previous results.
source: The results from this classification were broadly in line with our previous results.
evidence: This is a comparison of current results with previous work.

claim: Improved definition of the density in the cytoplasmic region enabled more accurate modeling of this region.
source: However, improved definition of the density in the cytoplasmic region enabled us to model this region more accurately.
evidence: This is a methodological observation from the current study.

claim: The position of the cytoplasmic region of TM2 in the maps correlated with the presence or absence of the N-terminus.
source: As before, the position of the cytoplasmic region of TM2 in these maps correlated with the presence or absence of the N-terminus.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis.

claim: Density associated with a hydrophobic molecule was present in the pore of both LMNG-NConst and LMNG-NFlex maps.
source: As observed in previous maps, density associated with a hydrophobic molecule was present in the pore of both maps (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density maps.

claim: For the LMNG-NConst conformation, the density for the side-chains of the residues of the N-terminus and the following link to TM1 is much clearer than seen in other maps.
source: For the LMNG-NConst conformation, the density for the side-chains of the residues of the N-terminus and the following link to TM1 is much clearer than seen in the other maps (Figure 1c), however it remains difficult to place the first three residues of the N-terminus unambiguously.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density maps.

claim: It remains difficult to place the first three residues of the N-terminus unambiguously in the LMNG-NConst structure.
source: For the LMNG-NConst conformation, the density for the side-chains of the residues of the N-terminus and the following link to TM1 is much clearer than seen in the other maps (Figure 1c), however it remains difficult to place the first three residues of the N-terminus unambiguously.
evidence: This is a limitation noted in the structural analysis.

claim: The LMNG-NConst structure is an advance on the previous structure of the equivalent conformation obtained in DDM (PDB 7QEW).
source: This new structure is an advance on the previous structure of the equivalent conformation obtained in DDM (PDB 7QEW) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current structure with a previous structure.

claim: In the LMNG-NConst structure, the N-terminal region of TM1 comprising residues Gly21 to Phe31 is rotated with respect to that modelled previously.
source: In the LMNG-NConst structure, the N-terminal region of TM1, preceding this area and comprising residues Gly21 to Phe31, is rotated with respect to that modelled previously, changing the position of the π-helix in TM1 from residues Ile20-Leu25 to residues Phe29-Val38 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the current study.

claim: The rotation of the N-terminal region of TM1 changes the position of the π-helix in TM1 from residues Ile20-Leu25 to residues Phe29-Val38.
source: In the LMNG-NConst structure, the N-terminal region of TM1, preceding this area and comprising residues Gly21 to Phe31, is rotated with respect to that modelled previously, changing the position of the π-helix in TM1 from residues Ile20-Leu25 to residues Phe29-Val38 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the current study.

claim: The conformation of TM1 in the LMNG-NConst structure differs from the crystal structures at both the N-terminal and C-terminal ends through variations in the twist of the helical repeats.
source: Thus, the conformation of TM1 in the LMNG-NConst structure differs from the crystal structures at both the N-terminal and C-terminal ends through variations in the twist of the helical repeats.
evidence: This is a structural comparison with previous crystal structures.

claim: In all structures of connexins solved to date, the cytoplasmic loop has been disordered.
source: In all structures of connexins solved to date, the cytoplasmic loop has been disordered.
evidence: This is a summary of observations from multiple published structures.

claim: For Cx26 the disordered cytoplasmic loop region extends from approximately residue Arg104 at the C-terminus of TM2 to Glu129 at the N-terminus of TM3.
source: For Cx26 this region extends from approximately residue Arg104 at the C-terminus of TM2 to Glu129 at the N-terminus of TM3.
evidence: This is a structural observation based on the protein sequence and structure.

claim: In the crystal structure (Cx26-xtal) residues 125–129 have been modelled as part of TM3.
source: In the crystal structure (Cx26-xtal) (Maeda et al., 2009) residues 125–129 have been modelled as part of TM3, whereas in our previous structures solved by cryo-EM (Brotherton et al., 2022) there was no evidence in the associated maps of the helix extending beyond Glu129.
evidence: This is a comparison with a published crystal structure.

claim: In previous cryo-EM structures there was no evidence in the associated maps of the helix extending beyond Glu129.
source: In the crystal structure (Cx26-xtal) (Maeda et al., 2009) residues 125–129 have been modelled as part of TM3, whereas in our previous structures solved by cryo-EM (Brotherton et al., 2022) there was no evidence in the associated maps of the helix extending beyond Glu129.
evidence: This is a comparison with the authors' previous work.

claim: Unassigned density protruded from near to the top of TM3 towards the loop between the N-terminus and TM1 in a manner that resembles models from AlphaFold2.
source: Instead, when analysing these maps it was noted that unassigned density protruded from near to the top of TM3 towards the loop between the N-terminus and TM1 in a manner that resembles models from AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al., 2021; Varadi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an observation from previous structural analysis compared with computational models.

claim: In the LMNG-NConst map the density for the C-terminal end of the cytoplasmic loop as it joins onto TM3 is much more clearly defined.
source: In the LMNG-NConst map this density is much more clearly defined as the C-terminal end of the cytoplasmic loop as it joins onto TM3 (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the current cryo-EM density maps.

claim: Residues Gln124 to Ile128, which form part of the K125VRIEG130 motif, were modelled into the density in the LMNG-NConst structure.
source: Residues Gln124 to Ile128, which form part of the K125VRIEG130 motif, important for carbamylation, were modelled into it, with Val126 located just above the linking region between the N-terminal helix and TM1 (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a structural modeling result from the current study.

claim: Val126 is located just above the linking region between the N-terminal helix and TM1 in the LMNG-NConst structure.
source: Residues Gln124 to Ile128, which form part of the K125VRIEG130 motif, important for carbamylation, were modelled into it, with Val126 located just above the linking region between the N-terminal helix and TM1 (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the current study.

claim: Lys125 in the LMNG-NConst structure is relatively close to the side-chain of Arg104 of the neighbouring subunit.
source: Though the density for the side-chains is poor and there is no definitive interaction, Lys125 in this position is relatively close to the side-chain of Arg104 of the neighbouring subunit, with which it had been proposed to form a salt bridge following carbamylation (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the current study.

claim: In the LMNG-NFlex map neither the N-terminus nor the KVRIEG motif are well defined.
source: By contrast, in the LMNG-NFlex map neither the N-terminus nor the KVRIEG motif are well defined (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density maps.

claim: The LMNG-NFlex map is reminiscent of the map derived from Cx26 particles vitrified under low PCO2 conditions.
source: The LMNG-NFlex map is reminiscent of the map derived from Cx26 particles vitrified under low PCO2 conditions (Brotherton et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a comparison with the authors' previous work.

claim: The conformational change in TM1 results in the side-chain of Trp24 rotating by ~90° between the two extreme positions.
source: The conformational change in TM1 results in the side-chain of Trp24 rotating by ~90° between the two extreme positions (Figure 2b, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparing the two conformations.

claim: At one extreme position, Trp24 faces the exterior of the protein and nestles a detergent or lipid tail.
source: At one of these extremes, it faces the exterior of the protein, and nestles a detergent or lipid tail.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the current study.

claim: At the other extreme position, Trp24 is within the core of the protein next to Arg143 and Ala88.
source: At the other extreme, it is within the core of the protein next to Arg143 and Ala88 (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the current study.

claim: The conformation in the NFlex structure would not be compatible with the position adopted by TM2 in the LMNG-NConst structure because Thr86 and Leu89 would clash with Phe31 and Ile30 on TM1 of the neighbouring subunit.
source: The conformation in the NFlex structure would not be compatible with the position adopted by TM2 in the LMNG-NConst structure because Thr86 and Leu89 would clash with Phe31 and Ile30 on TM1 of the neighbouring subunit (Figure 2b, Figure 2—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a structural analysis showing incompatibility between conformations.

claim: The rotation of TM1 changes not only how TM1 interacts with the N-terminus, but also the conformation of the linker between the N-terminal helix and TM1.
source: The rotation of TM1 changes not only how TM1 interacts with the N-terminus, but also the conformation of the linker between the N-terminal helix and TM1 (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the current study.

claim: The conformation of the linker between the N-terminal helix and TM1 would not be compatible with the conformation of the KVRIEG motif in LMNG-NConst.
source: This in turn would not be compatible with the conformation of the KVRIEG motif in LMNG-NConst (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a structural analysis showing incompatibility between conformations.

claim: The constriction of the channel by the N-terminal helix is associated with changes in the positions of TMs 1, 2 and the KVRIEG motif of the cytoplasmic loop.
source: Overall, therefore the constriction of the channel by the N-terminal helix is associated with changes in the positions of TMs 1, 2 and the KVRIEG motif of the cytoplasmic loop.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: Despite the LMNG-NConst map being much clearer for the cytoplasmic region of the protein, residues from 107 to 123 were still missing.
source: Despite the LMNG-NConst map being much clearer for the cytoplasmic region of the protein, residues from 107 to 123 were still missing.
evidence: This is an observation about the limitations of the structural data.

claim: In one classification case where the N-terminus was clearly defined, extra density was also seen for the cytoplasmic loop, albeit at low resolution.
source: Importantly, in one case and where the N-terminus was clearly defined, extra density was also seen for the cytoplasmic loop, albeit at low resolution.
evidence: This is an observation from the focused classification analysis.

claim: The structure was tentatively built into the density with the cytoplasmic loop of the classified subunit in a conformation resembling models from AlphaFold2.
source: The structure was tentatively built into the density with the cytoplasmic loop of the classified subunit in a conformation resembling models from AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al., 2021; Figure 3) and with a complete N-terminus (Table 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a structural modeling result from the current study.

claim: Only residues 109–114 were omitted in the final structure as the placement of these residues was ambiguous.
source: Only residues 109–114 were omitted in the final structure as the placement of these residues was ambiguous.
evidence: This is a note about the limitations of the structural model.

claim: There is density near to Lys125 that cannot be assigned, which may be a small molecule that has bound.
source: In the maps associated with this structure there is density that we cannot assign, near to Lys125, between Ser19 in the TM1-N-term linker, Tyr212 of TM4, and Tyr97 on TM3 of the neighbouring subunit, which may be a small molecule that has bound.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density maps with speculation about its identity.

claim: The conformation of the subunit in the focused classification is very similar to the LMNG-NConst structure with an RMSD of 0.38 Å for 198 Cα atoms.
source: Overall, the conformation of the subunit is very similar to the LMNG-NConst structure from the classification based on the masked hemichannels, with an RMSD of 0.38 Å for 198 Cα atoms.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of structural similarity.

claim: A second structure was refined that had a conformation much more similar to the LMNG-NFlex structure (RMSD 0.45 for 176 Cα atoms).
source: A second structure was also refined that had a conformation much more similar to the LMNG-NFlex structure (LMNG-NFlex-mon) (RMSD 0.45 for 176 Cα atoms) (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2, Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of structural similarity.

claim: Only the subunit upon which the focussed classification had been carried out had the NFlex-like conformation, with the density from the other subunits appearing more like the map before focussed classification.
source: Rather surprisingly, given the success of the hemichannel mask-based classification, only the subunit upon which the focussed classification had been carried out had this conformation, with the density from the other subunits appearing more like the map before focussed classification.
evidence: This is an observation from the focused classification analysis.

claim: When hexameric symmetry was applied to the subunit, steric clashes involving the N-terminal residues suggested a symmetric arrangement of this conformation would not be possible.
source: When hexameric symmetry was applied to the subunit, though the conformation of the N-terminus caused the aperture of the pore to appear closed, steric clashes involving the N-terminal residues suggested a symmetric arrangement of this conformation would not be possible (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a structural analysis showing incompatibility of symmetric arrangement.

claim: The analysis suggested a picture of a flexible molecule that can be captured in different conformations ranging from closed to open but with limited cooperativity between the subunits of the hexamer.
source: This analysis suggested a picture of a flexible molecule that can be captured in different conformations ranging from closed to open but with limited cooperativity between the subunits of the hexamer.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: For wild-type (WT) Cx26, gap junctions readily form between cells and allow rapid transfer of dye from a donor to a coupled acceptor cell at a PCO2 of 35 mmHg.
source: For wild-type (WT) Cx26, gap junctions readily form between cells and allow rapid transfer of dye from a donor (filled via a patch pipette) to a coupled acceptor cell at a PCO2 of 35 mmHg (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a result from the dye transfer assay.

claim: Cx26K125E forms structures that resemble WT gap junctions.
source: Cx26K125E forms structures that resemble WT gap junctions (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is an observation from the dye transfer assay.

claim: Cx26K125E gap junctions appeared to be shut and did not permit dye transfer at a PCO2 of 35 mmHg.
source: However, these gap junctions appeared to be shut and did not permit dye transfer at a PCO2 of 35 mmHg (Figure 4b and d).
evidence: This is a result from the dye transfer assay.

claim: Cx26K125E gap junctions remained closed at a PCO2 of 55 mmHg.
source: As the action of an increase in PCO2 is to close the WT Cx26 gap junction, unsurprisingly Cx26K125E gap junctions remained closed at a PCO2 of 55 mmHg (Figure 4c and d).
evidence: This is a result from the dye transfer assay.

claim: Purification of the K125E protein resulted in higher yields compared to the WT and K125R constructs, consistent with a more stable protein.
source: With respect to the WT and K125R constructs, purification of the K125E protein resulted in higher yields, consistent with a more stable protein.
evidence: This is an observation from the protein purification process.

claim: Refinement with D6 symmetry imposed resulted in maps with nominal resolutions of 2.2 and 2.1 Å for K125E and K125R respectively.
source: Refinement with D6 symmetry imposed resulted in maps with nominal resolutions of 2.2 and 2.1 Å respectively as defined by gold standard FSC (Rosenthal and Henderson, 2003; Scheres, 2012; Table 1, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a technical result from the cryo-EM data processing.

claim: There was a small but distinct change in the position of the cytoplasmic portion of TM2 between the K125E and K125R D6 averaged maps.
source: Superposition of the two maps showed there was a small but distinct change in the position of the cytoplasmic portion of TM2 between the two D6 averaged maps (Figure 5a and b, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This is a structural comparison result.

claim: The K125R map looked much more similar to the equivalent map from the WT protein purified in DDM and vitrified at the same PCO2.
source: Of the two, the K125R map looked much more similar to the equivalent map from the WT protein purified in the same way in DDM (PDB ID 7QEQ) and vitrified at the same PCO2 (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a structural comparison result.

claim: For the K125E data set the most populated class (43% of the particles) had a conformation similar to the LMNG-NConst.
source: For the K125E data set the most populated class (43% of the particles) had a conformation similar to the LMNG-NConst (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the focused classification analysis.

claim: Only 10% of the K125R data belonged to the class with conformation similar to LMNG-NConst.
source: In contrast only 10% of the data for the K125R belonged to this class (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a result from the focused classification analysis.

claim: Reconstructions from the most predominant class from the K125E data set (K125E90) have a nominal resolution of 2.5 Å.
source: Reconstructions from the most predominant class from the K125E data set (K125E90) have a nominal resolution of 2.5 Å (Table 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a technical result from the cryo-EM data processing.

claim: The KVRIEG motif and the N-terminus are reasonably well defined in the K125E90 density.
source: The KVRIEG motif and the N-terminus are reasonably well defined in the density as seen for the LMNG-NConst structure (Figure 5d) though again, the first three residues are difficult to position.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density maps.

claim: The K125E90 conformation is very similar to LMNG-NConst with an RMSD of 0.35 Å for 195 out of 199 matched Cα pairs.
source: Overall, the conformation is very similar to LMNG-NConst with an RMSD of 0.35 Å for 195 out of 199 matched Cα pairs (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of structural similarity.

claim: The RMSD of K125E90 compared to the LMNG-NFlex conformation is 2 Å across 180 Cα pairs.
source: In contrast the RMSD compared to the LMNG-NFlex conformation is 2 Å across 180 Cα pairs.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of structural similarity.

claim: The difference of the K125E maps from the equivalent maps from the WT and K125R proteins indicated a clear bias towards a more closed conformation of the protein in the CO2/HCO3- buffers.
source: The difference of the K125E maps from the equivalent maps from the WT and K125R proteins indicated a clear bias towards a more closed conformation of the protein in the CO2/HCO3- buffers.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural comparison results.

claim: The resolution of the maps was much lower for reconstructions from WT and K125E protein vitrified in HEPES buffer.
source: While the resolution of the maps was much lower for these reconstructions (Table 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 4) and better for the K125E mutant (4.2 Å) than the WT protein (4.9 Å) superposition of the respective maps again showed a movement of the cytoplasmic portion of TM2 together with a change in the N-terminus (Figure 5—figure supplement 5 and Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This is a technical result from the cryo-EM data processing.

claim: Superposition of the WT and K125E maps from HEPES buffer showed a movement of the cytoplasmic portion of TM2 together with a change in the N-terminus.
source: While the resolution of the maps was much lower for these reconstructions (Table 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 4) and better for the K125E mutant (4.2 Å) than the WT protein (4.9 Å) superposition of the respective maps again showed a movement of the cytoplasmic portion of TM2 together with a change in the N-terminus (Figure 5—figure supplement 5 and Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This is a structural comparison result.

claim: The K125E mutant is sufficient by itself to bias the conformation in the absence of CO2.
source: Thus, it appears that the K125E mutant is sufficient by itself to bias the conformation in the absence of CO2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data from HEPES buffer experiments.

claim: CO2 may have other effects on the protein to give the higher resolution and more defined conformation seen in the CO2/HCO3- buffers.
source: However, CO2 may have other effects on the protein to give the higher resolution and more defined conformation seen in the CO2/HCO3- buffers.
evidence: This is speculation based on the comparison of results in different buffer conditions.

claim: The improved data show that pore closure and the position of the N-terminal helix correlate with TM2, the conformation of TM1, and the KVRIEG motif on the regulatory cytoplasmic loop.
source: Our improved data show that, not only does pore closure and the position of the N-terminal helix correlate with TM2, but also with the conformation of TM1 and importantly, the KVRIEG motif on the regulatory cytoplasmic loop.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: In the NConst structures, the KVRIEG motif forms an extended conformation mimicking the conformations seen in AlphaFold2 structures.
source: In the NConst structures, the KVRIEG motif forms an extended conformation mimicking the conformations seen in AlphaFold2 structures.
evidence: This is a structural observation compared with computational models.

claim: The conformation of the complete loop observed in the subunit focussed classification is similar to that seen in AlphaFold2 structures.
source: In fact, the conformation of the complete loop that we observe in the subunit focussed classification is similar to that seen in AlphaFold2 structures (Varadi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a comparison with computational models.

claim: The KVRIEG motif can be described as a break in TM3 as the helix extends at either side of this extended motif.
source: Essentially the KVRIEG motif can be described as a break in TM3 as the helix extends at either side of this extended motif.
evidence: This is a structural interpretation.

claim: The position of TM2 seen in the NConst structures is an outlier compared to other connexin structures.
source: From a comparison of our structures with those of other connexins it is apparent that the position of TM2 seen in the NConst structures is an outlier, with a rotation of the cytoplasmic region of the helix compared to other structures (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a comparative structural analysis.

claim: The conformation of the Cx26-NConst structure most resembles the structures with N-down as these have similar conformations of TM1.
source: The conformation of the Cx26-NConst structure most resembles the structures with N-down as these have similar conformations of TM1 (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a comparative structural analysis.

claim: In structures with N-down, the N-terminus folds flat against the pore of the channel to give an open aperture.
source: However, whereas the N-terminus in these latter structures folds flat against the pore of the channel to give an open aperture, in the Cx26-NConst structure, it would be prevented from doing so by the position of TM2 and so is forced outwards to form a much more constricted aperture.
evidence: This is a comparative structural analysis.

claim: In the Cx26-NConst structure, the N-terminus is prevented from folding flat by the position of TM2 and is forced outwards to form a much more constricted aperture.
source: However, whereas the N-terminus in these latter structures folds flat against the pore of the channel to give an open aperture, in the Cx26-NConst structure, it would be prevented from doing so by the position of TM2 and so is forced outwards to form a much more constricted aperture.
evidence: This is a structural interpretation.

claim: The conformation of TM1 in the Cx26-NFlex structures is more similar to structures of other connexins in the N-flex or N-up conformations.
source: The conformation of TM1 in the Cx26-NFlex structures, which we consider to be open, is more similar to structures of other connexins in the N-flex or N-up conformations.
evidence: This is a comparative structural analysis.

claim: For Cx36 and Cx43, the N-flex or N-up conformations have been suggested to represent the closed conformation.
source: For Cx36 and Cx43 these conformations have been suggested to represent the closed conformation (Lee et al., 2023a; Qi et al., 2023a), though for Cx32 this has been described as an open conformation (Qi et al., 2023b).
evidence: This is a summary of interpretations from other published studies.

claim: For Cx32, the N-flex or N-up conformation has been described as an open conformation.
source: For Cx36 and Cx43 these conformations have been suggested to represent the closed conformation (Lee et al., 2023a; Qi et al., 2023a), though for Cx32 this has been described as an open conformation (Qi et al., 2023b).
evidence: This is a summary of interpretations from other published studies.

claim: In the Cx26-xtal structure, the N-terminus points into the pore, but the overall conformation is more similar to the Cx26-NFlex conformation.
source: The apparent outlier amongst the Cx26 structures is the Cx26-xtal structure where the N-terminus points into the pore, but the overall conformation is more similar to the Cx26-NFlex conformation.
evidence: This is a comparative structural analysis.

claim: Relative to the Cx26-NFlex structure, the N-terminal helix in Cx26-xtal is pulled back so is more open than seen in the Cx26-NConst structure.
source: However, relative to this latter structure the helix is pulled back (Figure 6b) so is more open than seen in the Cx26-NConst structure.
evidence: This is a comparative structural analysis.

claim: Similar density for a lipid-like molecule remains when the protein is solubilised with LMNG rather than DDM, strongly suggesting that this molecule cannot be detergent and is more likely to be a lipid.
source: The fact that similar density remains when the protein is solubilised with LMNG rather than DDM strongly suggests that this molecule cannot be detergent and is more likely to be a lipid.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of results with different detergents.

claim: A lipid-like molecule in the pore appears to be a constant feature of all the high-resolution cryo-EM maps associated with the structures of connexins where the N-terminus is not in the N-down position.
source: It is interesting to note that a lipid-like molecule in this position appears to be a constant feature of all the high-resolution cryo-EM maps associated with the structures of connexins where the N-terminus is not in the N-down position.
evidence: This is an observation based on comparison of multiple published structures.

claim: The lipid in the pore is only displaced when the N-terminus adopts the pore lining position.
source: It seems that the lipid is only displaced when the N-terminus adopts the pore lining position.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of multiple structures.

claim: In the Cx26-NConst structures, the lipid remains because the N-terminus cannot adopt the pore lining position due to the presence of TM2.
source: As this position is not possible in the Cx26-NConst structures due to the presence of TM2, the lipid remains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural analysis.

claim: With minor changes to the side-chains, the centre of the pore could be closed in the NConst structures.
source: It is difficult to model the first three residues of the N-terminus unambiguously, presumably due to the breakdown in sixfold symmetry at this point, but with minor changes to the side-chains, the centre of the pore could be closed.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural model.

claim: The presence of the lipid would seal any other apertures between the neighbouring N-termini.
source: The presence of the lipid would seal any other apertures between the neighbouring N-termini.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural model.

claim: Reconstructions of the full dodecamer following the focussed classifications of the single subunit do not show an influence of the conformation of that subunit on its neighbours.
source: Rather surprisingly given that we can isolate a symmetrical conformation of the protein using C6 symmetry, reconstructions of the full dodecamer following the focussed classifications of the single subunit do not show an influence of the conformation of that subunit on its neighbours.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis.

claim: The stochastic nature of the subunit conformations is consistent with structural studies on Cx43 gap junctions.
source: While this is consistent with structural studies on Cx43 gap junctions (Lee et al., 2023a) the stochastic nature of the subunit conformations contrasts with studies of Cx26 hemichannels in cell membranes where significant cooperativity has been observed (de Wolf et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison with other published studies.

claim: The stochastic nature of the subunit conformations contrasts with studies of Cx26 hemichannels in cell membranes where significant cooperativity has been observed.
source: While this is consistent with structural studies on Cx43 gap junctions (Lee et al., 2023a) the stochastic nature of the subunit conformations contrasts with studies of Cx26 hemichannels in cell membranes where significant cooperativity has been observed (de Wolf et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison with other published studies.

claim: There is a clear correlation between the results of the dye transfer assays and the structural results, supporting the interpretation that the NConst conformation is more like the closed state.
source: There is a clear correlation between the results of the dye transfer assays and the structural results, supporting the interpretation that the NConst conformation is more like the closed state.
evidence: This is an interpretation combining functional and structural data.

claim: The effect on the structure of Cx26 in changing K125 to a glutamate both in CO2/HCO3- and in HEPES buffer is consistent with the hypothesis that the CO2-mediated closure of the gap junctions is caused by the carbamylation of K125.
source: The effect on the structure of Cx26 in changing K125 to a glutamate both in CO2/HCO3- and in HEPES buffer is consistent with the hypothesis that the CO2-mediated closure of the gap junctions is caused by the carbamylation of K125.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data in support of a hypothesis.

claim: Even under high PCO2 conditions the WT protein is not completely carbamylated during vitrification.
source: It would also suggest that even under high PCO2 conditions the WT protein is not completely carbamylated during vitrification.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: Given that the carbamylation reaction is highly labile, incomplete carbamylation during vitrification is not surprising.
source: Given that the carbamylation reaction is highly labile, this is perhaps not surprising.
evidence: This is reasoning based on the chemical properties of carbamylation.

claim: Mutation of Arg104 to alanine abolishes CO2 sensitivity in both GJCs and hemichannels.
source: Consistent with this, mutation of Arg104 to alanine abolishes CO2 sensitivity in both GJCs (Nijjar et al., 2021) and hemichannels (Meigh et al., 2013), similar to the mutation of Lys125.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: In models from AlphaFold2, the lysine is located next to the arginine.
source: In models from AlphaFold2, which differ in conformation from the structure upon which the hypothesis was based, it is also notable that the lysine is located next to the arginine (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is an observation from computational models.

claim: In the NConst structures the position of the Lys/Glu125 main chain is near to Arg104, even though TM2 moves further from TM3 in moving from the NFlex to the NConst conformations.
source: In the NConst structures the position of the Lys/Glu125 main chain is near to Arg104, even though TM2 moves further from TM3 in moving from the NFlex to the NConst conformations.
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: There is no clear interaction between Lys/Glu125 and Arg104 in the NConst structures.
source: Though there is no clear interaction between the two residues, with minor adjustments of the side-chains, the residues could be made to interact and the absence of a definite interaction may be due to distortions during the vitrification process or radiation damage to which acidic residues are more prone.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis with speculation about the reasons.

claim: Glutamate is much shorter than the carbamylated lysine, so that while the charges would be equivalent, the two residues might not be able to make the same specific interactions.
source: Glutamate is also much shorter than the carbamylated lysine, so that while the charges would be equivalent, the two residues might not be able to make the same specific interactions.
evidence: This is reasoning based on the chemical structures of the residues.

claim: The results show that the negative charge at residue 125 is important for altering conformation.
source: Our results here show that the negative charge at residue 125 is important for altering conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the structural data.

claim: For hemichannels, a direct interaction between R104 and K125 is strongly supported by a mutant in which both residues are replaced by cysteines, allowing a potential cross-link through a disulphide bond.
source: For hemichannels, a direct interaction between the two residues (Meigh et al., 2015) is strongly supported by a mutant in which both R104 and K125 are replaced by cysteines, allowing a potential cross-link through a disulphide bond.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The double cysteine mutant (R104C/K125C) responds to a change in redox potential in a similar way to which the WT protein responds to CO2.
source: This mutant responds to a change in redox potential in a similar way to which the WT protein responds to CO2 (Meigh et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Both Lys125 and Arg104 are necessary for CO2-dependent gap junction closure.
source: However, although both Lys125 and Arg104 are necessary for CO2-dependent gap junction closure, attributing the induction of the conformational change in the gap junction to a single salt bridge between Lys125 and Arg104 may be an over-simplification.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural and functional data.

claim: Attributing the induction of the conformational change in the gap junction to a single salt bridge between Lys125 and Arg104 may be an over-simplification.
source: However, although both Lys125 and Arg104 are necessary for CO2-dependent gap junction closure, attributing the induction of the conformational change in the gap junction to a single salt bridge between Lys125 and Arg104 may be an over-simplification.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: There may be other interactions involved in CO2-dependent gap junction closure.
source: For example, there may be other interactions involved and it is possible that multiple carbamylation events contribute to gap junction sensitivity (Brotherton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation.

claim: It is possible that multiple carbamylation events contribute to gap junction sensitivity.
source: For example, there may be other interactions involved and it is possible that multiple carbamylation events contribute to gap junction sensitivity (Brotherton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation.

claim: Some protein is observed in the NConst conformation even when Arg125 is mutated to arginine.
source: Given that we observe some protein in the NConst conformation even when Arg125 is mutated to arginine, our data would be consistent with a conformationally flexible protein, in which the introduction of a negative charge would stabilise one particular conformation, rather than causing a conformational change per se (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an observation from the structural data.

claim: The data are consistent with a conformationally flexible protein, in which the introduction of a negative charge would stabilise one particular conformation, rather than causing a conformational change per se.
source: Given that we observe some protein in the NConst conformation even when Arg125 is mutated to arginine, our data would be consistent with a conformationally flexible protein, in which the introduction of a negative charge would stabilise one particular conformation, rather than causing a conformational change per se (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The position of Ala88, mutation of which to Val causes KIDS, is at the flexion point of TM2.
source: While these mutations have been mapped on the structure previously, the position of Ala88, mutation of which to Val causes KIDS, is interesting with regard to the new conformations of TM1. This mutation, which is at the flexion point of TM2 (Figure 2b), results in leaky hemichannels (Mhaske et al., 2013) and has been shown to prevent CO2 sensitivity either to the gap junctions, in closing the channels (Nijjar et al., 2021), or to the hemichannels in opening the protein (Meigh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a structural observation with reference to disease-causing mutations.

claim: The A88V mutation results in leaky hemichannels.
source: This mutation, which is at the flexion point of TM2 (Figure 2b), results in leaky hemichannels (Mhaske et al., 2013) and has been shown to prevent CO2 sensitivity either to the gap junctions, in closing the channels (Nijjar et al., 2021), or to the hemichannels in opening the protein (Meigh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The A88V mutation has been shown to prevent CO2 sensitivity in gap junctions.
source: This mutation, which is at the flexion point of TM2 (Figure 2b), results in leaky hemichannels (Mhaske et al., 2013) and has been shown to prevent CO2 sensitivity either to the gap junctions, in closing the channels (Nijjar et al., 2021), or to the hemichannels in opening the protein (Meigh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The A88V mutation has been shown to prevent CO2 sensitivity in hemichannels.
source: This mutation, which is at the flexion point of TM2 (Figure 2b), results in leaky hemichannels (Mhaske et al., 2013) and has been shown to prevent CO2 sensitivity either to the gap junctions, in closing the channels (Nijjar et al., 2021), or to the hemichannels in opening the protein (Meigh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: In the NConst structures the Cβ of Ala88 lies within 4.2 Å of Trp24, which moves during the conformational change of TM1.
source: In the Nconst structures the Cβ of Ala88 lies within 4.2 Å of Trp24, which moves during the conformational change of TM1.
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: Replacement of Ala88 with the bulkier valine would hinder the NConst conformation from being adopted and therefore would disfavour the closed conformation.
source: Replacement of the alanine with the bulkier valine would hinder this conformation from being adopted and therefore, would disfavour the closed conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural analysis.

claim: Ala88 and Trp24 are located next to Arg143.
source: Interestingly, the alanine and the tryptophan are located next to Arg143.
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: Mutation of Arg143 to tryptophan is a very common mutation that leads to non-syndromic hearing loss.
source: Mutation of Arg143 to tryptophan is a very common mutation that leads to non-syndromic hearing loss (Xu and Nicholson, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published review.

claim: The data provide important mechanistic insight into the conformational changes behind pore closure in Cx26, which is useful for understanding how mutations in the protein can lead to disease.
source: Overall our data, summarised in Figure 7, provide important mechanistic insight into the conformational changes behind pore closure in Cx26, which is useful for understanding how mutations in the protein can lead to disease.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's significance.
